title: Louise Cowan’s Speech on Teachers, Part II
author: Louise Cowan
summary: In the second half of a speech to Dallas-area teachers, Louise Cowan argues that the word virtue has been replaced in public life by the relativistic word value, and that teachers must recover the older idea of a moral law written on the human heart. She says the primary aim of education is preserving and transmitting the body of knowledge and virtue that produced civilization, with student development a secondary by-product. Teachers are therefore representatives of a culture who need an education in the best that has been thought and said. As screens and artificial constructions multiply, schools will have to teach what it is to be human, and democracy itself must be taught. She closes by honoring the Dallas Institute Teachers Academy and urging that its model be taken to more cities.
points: Replacing the word virtue with value reduces moral ideals to private preferences and undermines the sense that the moral law is universal.
The primary purpose of education is the preservation and transmission of civilization's wisdom, with student development a secondary by-product.
Teachers are the medium through which the present contacts the past, so teacher education must give them direct acquaintance with the great thinkers.
In an age of information and technology, schools must teach what it is to be human, including love, loyalty, faith, hope and virtue.
Democracy does not come naturally and must be taught by teachers who know the heritage that sustains it.
quotes: But “value” implies a quality given to a person or a thing by our preferences: that is, we value particular objects or particular ways of behaving.
For teachers are the representatives of a culture. Their task is primarily to ensure the passing on of the wisdom—the knowledge and virtues—of a people.

We mistake our educational aims when we consider our task to be primarily the development of the student: that is only a secondary purpose, the primary one being the preservation of that body of knowledge that has produced the precious gift of civilization.

The enemy of education is barbarism; the teacher’s duty is thus to fight off that ever-present menace by preserving and transmitting the heritage of freedom and virtue that has come to us from the past but which is always open to new insights and to new communities of people.
Above all else, however, we shall have to teach what it is to be human, what it is to love parents and friends, to revere our nation and the world
Teacher education must be radically changed, for teachers are the medium through which the present makes contact with the past, while anticipating the future.
Democracy has to be taught. Only the instruction of our young in wisdom and virtue can sustain the remarkable system of government envisioned by our founders.
